en:google_translate.text: A towering building stands in the northwest,
Its heights level with the drifting clouds.
Latticed windows feature intricate, patterned carvings,
And the pavilion rises in three-tiered terraces.
From above come the sounds of strings and song—
How deeply sorrowful the melody rings!
Who could have composed such a tune?
Surely, it must be the wife of Qi Liang.
The *Qingshang* notes rise upon the breeze,
Lingering and wavering in the mid-melody.
With every strum come repeated sighs,
A stirring passion steeped in lingering grief.
It is not the singer's toil that brings such pain,
But the scarcity of those who truly understand the music.
Oh, to become a pair of soaring swans,
And beat our wings to take flight on high.

en:waley_1918.text: In the north-west there is a high house,
Its top level with the floating clouds.
Embroidered curtains thinly screen its windows,
Its storied tower is built on three steps.
From above there comes a noise of playing and singing,
The tune sounding, oh! how sad!
Who can it be, playing so sad a tune?
Surely it must be Ch’i Liang’s wife.
The tranquil “D” follows the wind’s rising,
To each note, two or three sobs,
Her high will conquered by overwhelming grief.
She does not regret that she is left so sad,
But minds that so few can understand her song.
She wants to become those two wild geese
That with beating wings rise high aloft.
